scope_note: Family-recognition backfill for the Hays/Central Texas learner. Expands the family from the previously mapped Cephalanthus-only view to the actual local source pool of Cephalanthus plus Galium, while retaining Galium aparine as an introduced local comparison rather than a native metric.

actions: Restored Gentianales / Rubiaceae to Cephalanthus occidentalis.
Restored Gentianales / Rubiaceae to Galium aparine, G. texense, and G. virgatum.
Added Galium -> Rubiaceae to the hidden genus-family map; Cephalanthus was already mapped.
Flagged Galium aparine as a non-native local comparison under current POWO treatment; retain for field training but exclude from native metrics.
Confirmed current accepted concepts for Cephalanthus occidentalis, Galium texense, and Galium virgatum.

family_lesson.where_to_look_first: Start at the node, not the flower. Rubiaceae typically has simple opposite or whorled leaves plus interpetiolar stipules sitting between the petiole bases. Then confirm a fused tubular/rotate corolla, stamens matching the corolla-lobe number, and an inferior ovary.
family_lesson.strongest_field_confirmation: Opposite/whorled simple leaves + interpetiolar stipules + sympetalous mostly radial flower + stamens equal in number to corolla lobes + inferior ovary.
core_characters: Trees, shrubs, herbs or climbers; local anchors range from woody buttonbush to tiny annual bedstraws.
Leaves simple, usually opposite or whorled.
Interpetiolar stipules are a major family character; in Galium they become leaf-like and contribute to the apparent whorl.
Corolla fused, usually radial, commonly 4- or 5-lobed.
Stamens usually equal the number of corolla lobes and alternate with them.
Fruit varies greatly: drupaceous or berry-like fruits, capsules, schizocarps and mericarps all occur.
Stipules may bear colleters/glandular tips; these are useful close-up characters.
avoid_overgeneralizing: Do not use opposite leaves alone: Oleaceae, Verbenaceae, Lamiaceae and several other families also have opposite leaves.
Do not assume stipules always look like tiny separate flaps; in Galium they can be leaf-like and nearly indistinguishable from the true leaves.
Do not teach Rubiaceae fruit as one type; buttonbush and bedstraw have very different fruit architecture.
Do not count Galium aparine as native under current POWO treatment even though it is common and wild locally.
Do not rely on square stems: Galium can be 4-angled, but that character also occurs in Lamiaceae/Verbenaceae.

node_lesson.key_point: The node is the family checkpoint.
node_lesson.Cephalanthus: Opposite or whorled true leaves with obvious triangular stipules between adjacent petiole bases.
node_lesson.Galium: The apparent whorl includes true leaves plus leaf-like stipules; visually, the node looks like 4–8 leaf-like units radiating from the stem.
node_lesson.teaching_rule: For Rubiaceae, ask 'what is between the petioles?' before asking 'what color is the flower?'

fastest_cues: Leaves opposite or in whorls of 3–4.
Dense spherical heads of many tiny white tubular flowers.
Styles project far outward, producing the pincushion/button look.
Inferior ovaries mature into a dense spherical fruiting head.
Cephalanthus.teaching_anchor: Best woody Rubiaceae anchor and best interpetiolar-stipule + inferior-ovary demonstration.

fastest_cues: Leaf-like units arranged in apparent whorls.
Whorl partly consists of enlarged leaf-like stipules.
Several species use hairs/prickles on stems, leaf margins, or fruits as major ID characters.
Galium.teaching_anchor: Best example showing how stipules can masquerade as leaves.

fast_key: Opposite/whorled simple leaves + obvious interpetiolar stipules -> strongly consider Rubiaceae.
Wetland shrub + spherical white pincushion flower heads + stipules between petioles -> Cephalanthus occidentalis.
Tiny herb + apparent leaf whorls + 4-angled stem + tiny 4-part flowers -> Galium.
Whorls of 6–8 + backward-facing hooked prickles + sticky paired burr-like fruits -> Galium aparine introduced comparison.
Whorls of 4 + ovate small leaves + hairy stems + hooked fruit bristles -> Galium texense.
Whorls of 4 + tiny narrow leaves + mostly non-hooked stem + small local annual -> Galium virgatum.
Opposite woody leaves but no interpetiolar stipules + superior ovary -> reconsider Oleaceae.

stipule_lesson.title: Interpetiolar stipules — the Rubiaceae giveaway
stipule_lesson.Cephalanthus_visual: Show two opposite petioles and circle the small triangular stipule sitting between them.
stipule_lesson.Galium_visual: Show a node with four or more leaf-like units and explain that some of the 'leaves' are actually enlarged foliar stipules.
stipule_lesson.memory_line: Rubiaceae often puts something between the petioles.

ovary_lesson.key_point: The ovary is inferior: the corolla and calyx appear to arise from above the ovary/young fruit.
ovary_lesson.Cephalanthus_visual: Use a side-view individual flower from the spherical head and label the inferior ovary below the corolla tube.
ovary_lesson.Galium_visual: Use a tiny flower/young fruit macro and label the paired ovary lobes below the rotate corolla.
ovary_lesson.tie_breaker: This inferior ovary is a strong separator from Oleaceae, Verbenaceae and Lamiaceae, which have superior ovaries.

fruit_lesson.Cephalanthus: Many flowers in one spherical head mature into many small dry fruit units; the whole brown ball is an infructescence, not one fruit.
fruit_lesson.Galium: The 2-lobed inferior ovary matures into a schizocarp that separates into 2 one-seeded mericarps.
fruit_lesson.aparine_special: Hooked fruit hairs turn the mericarps into hitchhikers on clothing and animal fur.

Oleaceae.confusion: Opposite woody leaves can look very similar before flowering.
Oleaceae.tie_breaker: Rubiaceae has interpetiolar stipules and an inferior ovary. Oleaceae is exstipulate and has a superior ovary; local Oleaceae also has samaras or 1-seeded drupes.

Verbenaceae.confusion: Opposite leaves, sometimes 4-angled stems and small clustered flowers.
Verbenaceae.tie_breaker: Verbenaceae lacks the defining interpetiolar stipules and has a superior ovary; fruit architecture is also different.

Lamiaceae.confusion: Opposite leaves and square stems, especially compared with Galium.
Lamiaceae.tie_breaker: Lamiaceae lacks interpetiolar stipules and usually has a deeply 4-lobed superior ovary yielding 4 nutlets; Rubiaceae has an inferior ovary.
